title.zh: 卷三十一 列傳第一 后妃上
title.en: Volume 31 Biographies 1: Empresses and Consorts Part One
title.raw: 卷三十一 列傳第一 后妃上 Volume 31 Biographies 1: Empresses and Consorts Part One

sentences.zh: 夫乾坤定位，男女流形，伉儷之義同歸，貴賤之名異等。

translations.literal: As for Qian and Kun taking their positions, male and female receive their forms; the principle of husband and wife aims at the same end, yet the names of noble and base stand in different ranks.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth fixed their stations; men and women took their bodily shapes. Husband and wife share one moral purpose, even though rank divides high from low.

sentences.zh: 若乃作配皇極，齊體紫宸，象玉床之連後星，喻金波之合羲璧。

translations.literal: When one is paired with the supreme apex and shares the substance of the Purple Palace, it is likened to the jade couch linking to the rear stars, and compared to golden waves joining the Xi disk.
translations.idiomatic: Those who match the sovereign on high and share the body politic of the inner palace are figured as the jade couch tied to the queen’s asterism, as moonlight married to the solar disk.

translations.literal: From remote antiquity onward, she was called the chief consort;
translations.idiomatic: In deepest antiquity she was known as the principal wife;

translations.literal: Descending to middle antiquity, she was then titled queen.
translations.idiomatic: Later ages styled her queen.

sentences.zh: 四人並列，光于帝嚳之宮；

translations.literal: Four women stood ranked together, shining in the palace of Emperor Ku;
translations.idiomatic: Four consorts stood side by side and brought glory to Emperor Ku’s inner court;

sentences.zh: 二妃同降，著彼有虞之典。

translations.literal: Two consorts descended together, written into the canons of Yu’s age.
translations.idiomatic: Two royal brides arrived together and entered the canonical record of Shun’s reign.

sentences.zh: 夏商以上，六宮之制，其詳靡得而聞焉。

translations.literal: Above Xia and Shang, the regulations of the Six Palaces cannot be heard of in detail.
translations.idiomatic: For ages before Xia and Shang, no reliable detail survives about how the six wings of the harem were ordered.

sentences.zh: 姬劉以降，五翟之規，其事可略而言矣。

translations.literal: From Ji and Liu onward, the rules of the five pheasant insignia may be spoken of in outline.
translations.idiomatic: From the Zhou and Han dynasties on, the graded “five pheasant” ritual for consorts can at least be sketched.

sentences.zh: 周禮，天子立一后、三夫人、九嬪、二十七世婦、八十一御妻，以聽王者內政。

translations.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, the Son of Heaven establishes one queen, three ladies, nine bin, twenty-seven wives of rank, and eighty-one minor wives, to administer the king’s inner administration.
translations.idiomatic: The Rites of Zhou prescribe one empress, three chief consorts, nine ranked ladies, twenty-seven secondary wives, and eighty-one attendants to manage the sovereign’s domestic government.

sentences.zh: 故婚義曰：「天子之與后，如日之與月，陰之與陽。

translations.literal: Therefore the Meaning of Marriage says: “The Son of Heaven and the queen are like sun and moon, yin and yang.
translations.idiomatic: The Meaning of Marriage therefore declares: “The emperor and his empress mirror sun and moon, yin and yang.”

translations.literal: ” From this perspective, what they derive from is distant indeed.
translations.idiomatic: ” Judged by such language, their institution reaches far back into antiquity.

sentences.zh: 故能母儀天宇，助宣王化，德均載物，比大坤維，宗廟歆其薦羞，穹壤俟其交泰。

translations.literal: Thus she can be the motherly model for all under heaven, aid in spreading royal transformation, her virtue evenly bearing all things, comparable to the great sustaining power of Kun; the ancestral temple delights in her offerings, heaven and earth await her harmonizing union.
translations.idiomatic: Hence she sets the maternal standard for the realm, advances the king’s civilizing work, and bears creation as steadfastly as earth itself; the temple accepts her sacrifices gladly, and heaven and earth look to her union with the throne for peace.

sentences.zh: 是以哲王垂憲，尤重造舟之禮；

translations.literal: Therefore wise kings hang forth statutes and especially esteem the rite of the built bridge;
translations.idiomatic: That is why enlightened monarchs codify law and prize above all the royal wedding rite of “meeting across the boat.”

sentences.zh: 詩人立言，先獎葛覃之訓。

translations.literal: The poets set forth words and first praise the instruction of “Ge Tan.”
translations.idiomatic: The Classic of Poetry opens by honoring the lessons of “Ge Tan,” the ode on diligent royal ladies.

sentences.zh: 後燭流景，所以裁其宴私；

translations.literal: The rear candle’s flowing light is the means to regulate their private banquets;
translations.idiomatic: Dimming the late-night lamp curbs excess in the privy chamber;

sentences.zh: 房樂希聲，是用節其容止。

translations.literal: Chamber music with sparse sound is the means to moderate their bearing.
translations.idiomatic: Sparse music in the inner rooms reins in conduct at court and couch alike.

translations.literal: Walking upright to rectify the root—is this not what is meant!
translations.idiomatic: Walking straight to set the root right—surely this is what those measures intend!

sentences.zh: 若乃娉納有方，防閑有禮，肅尊儀而修四德，體柔範而弘六義，陰教洽于宮闈，淑譽騰於區域。

translations.literal: If betrothal and intake have proper method, fences and restraint have ritual, reverently honoring ceremony while cultivating the four virtues, embodying gentle norms while extending the six meanings, then women’s instruction permeates the palace, and good reputation rises through the regions.
translations.idiomatic: When matches are arranged by rule, propriety fences passion, majesty guards ritual while the four womanly virtues are cultivated, gentle models enlarge the six canonical lessons, inner-chamber teaching fills the harem, and fair fame spreads beyond the capital.

sentences.zh: 則玄雲入戶，上帝錫母萌之符；

translations.literal: Then dark clouds enter the door, and the Supreme Lord grants the sign of motherhood’s sprouting;
translations.idiomatic: Then auspicious clouds cross the threshold and Heaven grants the token of fruitful motherhood;

sentences.zh: 黃神降徵，坤靈贊壽丘之道，終能鼎祚惟永，胤嗣克昌。

translations.literal: The Yellow Spirit sends down omens; the spirit of Kun assists the way of Shouqiu; ultimately the tripod fortune can be everlasting and heirs flourish.
translations.idiomatic: The divine Yellow Emperor sends portents; earth’s spirit blesses the birth-hill of sage-kings; the dynasty’s mandate endures and heirs thrive.

sentences.zh: 至若儷極虧閑，憑天作孽，倒裳衣于衽席，感朓側於弦望。

translations.literal: As for those paired to the apex yet deficient in restraint, who rely on heaven to work calamity, who overturn upper and lower garments upon the mat, and feel lust askew at first quarter and full moon.
translations.idiomatic: But women who reach the throne yet abandon modesty, who invoke Heaven while plotting harm, who turn proper dress upside down on the bed, and whose passions shift with every phase of the moon—

sentences.zh: 則龍漦結釁，宗周鞠為黍苗；

translations.literal: Then dragon-spittle knots disaster, and royal Zhou becomes nothing but millet shoots;
translations.idiomatic: —dragon spit seals a fatal feud, and the Zhou heartland turns to weed-grown ruin;

sentences.zh: 燕尾挻災，隆漢墜其枌社矣。

translations.literal: Swallow tails draw calamity, and flourishing Han drops its mulberry altars.
translations.idiomatic: swallow-tail charms invite catastrophe, and even mighty Han loses its soil-and-millet shrines.

sentences.zh: 自曹劉內主，位以色登，甄衛之家，榮非德舉。

translations.literal: Since the inner mistresses of Cao and Liu, position climbed by beauty; in the households of Zhen and Wei, glory was not raised by virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Under the Cao and Liu courts, palace ladies rose by looks alone; clans such as the Zhens and Weis won favor without moral merit.

sentences.zh: 淫荒挺性，蔑西郊之禮容；

translations.literal: Dissolute and wasteful by nature, they slighted the ritual bearing of the western suburb;
translations.idiomatic: Wanton temperaments mocked the solemn suburban liturgy reserved for the empress;

sentences.zh: 婉孌含辭，作南國之奇態。

translations.literal: Soft loveliness holding coy phrases, they fashioned exotic manners of the southern states.
translations.idiomatic: Soft voices and studied phrases invented the freakish grace of southern entertainers.

sentences.zh: 詖謁由斯外人，穢德於是內宣。

translations.literal: Slanderous flattery thereby passed outward, and foul conduct was proclaimed within.
translations.idiomatic: Sycophancy leaked beyond the palace gates while depravity was preached inside.

sentences.zh: 椒掖播晨牝之風，蘭殿絕河雎之響。

translations.literal: The pepper chambers spread the wind of the hen crowing at dawn; the orchid halls cut off the echo of “Guan ju” by the River.
translations.idiomatic: The harem aired the omen of women ruling like crowing hens; orchid halls no longer echoed the chaste songs of “Guan ju.”

sentences.zh: 永言彤史，大練之範逾微；

translations.literal: Speaking long of the vermilion scribe, the model of coarse white silk grows ever fainter;
translations.idiomatic: Forever the palace diarists wrote, yet the ideal of homespun austerity faded;

sentences.zh: 緬視青蒲，脫珥之猷替矣。

translations.literal: Gazing afar at the green rushes, the strategy of casting off ear-jewels is replaced.
translations.idiomatic: Looking back to mat audiences where consorts remonstrated, the counsel of tearing off earrings to warn the throne had vanished.

sentences.zh: 晉承其末，與世污隆，宣皇創基，功弘而道屈；

translations.literal: Jin inherited the late age; with the world it sank and rose. Emperor Xuan founded the base—achievement broad yet the Way bent;
translations.idiomatic: The Jin took up this fallen era and rose or fell with the times. Emperor Xuan laid the foundations: his deeds were grand, yet the moral course stayed cramped;

translations.literal: one goodness of Empress Mu—merit equal to the Ten Disorderly Ones.
translations.idiomatic: a single virtue in Empress Mu rivaled the merit of the “ten turbulent” worthies who saved a dynasty.

sentences.zh: 洎乎世祖，[1]始親選良家，既而帝掩紈扇，躬行請託。

translations.literal: Down to Shizu [1], he began personally selecting from good families; thereafter the emperor hid behind the silk fan and personally practiced solicitation.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Wu [1] the court at first picked brides from respectable houses; soon the sovereign waved his silk fan in the inner quarters and himself traded favors for appointments.

sentences.zh: 后採長白，實彰妒忌之情；

translations.literal: The empress chose “long white,” truly displaying jealousy;
translations.idiomatic: An empress chosen for graying hair laid bare the spite of jealousy;

sentences.zh: 賈納短青，竟踐覆亡之轍。

translations.literal: Jia took in “short green,” and in the end trod the rut of overthrow.
translations.idiomatic: the Jias welcomed a young rival and eventually followed the same rut to ruin.

sentences.zh: 得失遺跡，煥在綈緗，興滅所由，義同畫一。

translations.literal: Tracks of gain and loss shine forth on silk documents; the causes of rise and ruin share one uniform pattern in meaning.
translations.idiomatic: Success and failure still gleam from the silk-bound histories; the springs of fortune and disaster follow one clear pattern.

sentences.zh: 故列其本事，以為后妃傳云。

translations.literal: Therefore I array their basic affairs to form this treatise on empresses and consorts.
translations.idiomatic: I therefore set out the essential facts as this “Treatise on Empresses and Consorts.”

translations.literal: Empress Zhang Xuanmu
translations.idiomatic: Empress Zhang the August and Revered

sentences.zh: 宣穆張皇后諱春華，河內平皋人也。

translations.literal: Empress Zhang Xuanmu, taboo name Chunhua, was a native of Pinggao in Henei.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Zhang Xuanmu, personal name Chunhua, came from Pinggao in Henei commandery.

translations.literal: Her father Wang was magistrate of Suiyi in Wei;
translations.idiomatic: Her father Wang had served as magistrate of Suiyi under Wei;

sentences.zh: 母河內山氏，司徒濤之從祖姑也。

translations.literal: her mother was a Shan of Henei, a paternal grand-aunt by cousinship of Minister of Education Tao.
translations.idiomatic: her mother was a Shan from Henei, first cousin once removed to Grand Tutor Shan Tao.

sentences.zh: 后少有德行，智識過人，生景帝、文帝、平原王幹、南陽公主。

translations.literal: The empress from youth had virtuous conduct and intelligence surpassing others; she bore Emperor Jing, Emperor Wen, Prince Gan of Pingyuan, and the Princess of Nanyang.
translations.idiomatic: She showed virtue and unusual discernment from girlhood. She was mother to Emperors Jing and Wen, to Prince Sima Gan of Pingyuan, and to the Princess of Nanyang.

sentences.zh: 宣帝初辭魏武之命，託以風痹，嘗暴書，遇暴雨，不覺自起收之。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuan at first declined Wei Wu’s summons, pleading wind paralysis, he once sunned books; encountering a sudden storm, unthinkingly he rose himself to gather them in.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan first refused Cao Cao’s summons, claiming crippling palsy, he once aired books in the sun. A cloudburst came; forgetting his act, he leapt up to rescue them.

sentences.zh: 家惟有一婢見之，后乃恐事泄致禍，遂手殺之以滅口，而親自執爨。

translations.literal: Only one maid in the house saw it; the empress then feared the affair leaking and bringing disaster, so she personally killed her to silence her, and herself attended the cooking stove.
translations.idiomatic: A single bondmaid witnessed it. Fearing exposure would destroy them, the empress killed her with her own hands and herself cooked the family meals to hide the truth.

translations.literal: The emperor from this esteemed her.
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter her husband valued her all the more.

sentences.zh: 其後柏夫人有寵，后罕得進見。

translations.literal: Afterward Lady Bai had favor, and the empress rarely obtained audience.
translations.idiomatic: Later Lady Bai won his favor, and the empress was seldom admitted.

translations.literal: The emperor once lay ill; the empress went to inquire after his illness.
translations.idiomatic: Once when he lay sick, she came to nurse him.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「老物可憎，何煩出也！

translations.literal: The emperor said: “That old creature is hateful—why trouble to come out!
translations.idiomatic: He snapped, “That foul old hag—why drag herself here!”

sentences.zh: 」后慚恚不食，將自殺，諸子亦不食。

translations.literal: ” The empress, ashamed and enraged, did not eat and was about to kill herself; her sons likewise did not eat.
translations.idiomatic: ” Shamed and furious, she refused food and meant to take her life; her sons fasted with her.

translations.literal: The emperor was alarmed and apologized; the empress then stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Alarmed, he apologized, and she gave up the attempt.

sentences.zh: 帝退而謂人曰：「老物不足惜，慮困我好兒耳！」

translations.literal: The emperor withdrew and said to someone: “The old creature is not worth pity—I worry she will distress my good sons!”
translations.idiomatic: Privately he muttered, “I care nothing for the hag—I fear only harm to my fine sons.”

sentences.zh: 魏正始八年崩，時年五十九，葬洛陽高原陵，追贈廣平縣君。

translations.literal: She died in Wei’s eighth Zhengshi year, aged fifty-nine, buried at Gaoyuan tumulus in Luoyang, posthumously endowed as Lady of Guangping County.
translations.idiomatic: She died in 247 at fifty-nine and was buried at Gaoyuan mausoleum east of Luoyang; Wei later enfeoffed her posthumously as Lady of Guangping.

translations.literal: In the first Xianxi year she was posthumously titled Consort Xuanmu.
translations.idiomatic: In 264 she received the posthumous title Consort Xuanmu.

sentences.zh: 及武帝受禪，追尊為皇后。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu received the abdication, she was posthumously honored as empress.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu took the throne, she was raised posthumously to empress.

translations.literal: Empress Xiahou Jinghuai
translations.idiomatic: Empress Xiahou the Revered and Cherished

sentences.zh: 景懷夏侯皇后諱徽，字媛容，沛國譙人也。

translations.literal: Empress Xiahou Jinghuai, taboo name Hui, courtesy name Yuanrong, was a native of Qiao in Pei.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Xiahou Jinghuai, personal name Hui, courtesy name Yuanrong, came from Qiao in the state of Pei.

translations.literal: Her father Shang was Grand General Who Conquers the South in Wei;
translations.idiomatic: Her father Xiahou Shang held Wei’s post of Grand General Who Conquers the South;

translations.literal: her mother was a Cao, Village Mistress of Deyang in Wei.
translations.idiomatic: her mother was a daughter of the Wei imperial house, titled Village Mistress of Deyang.

sentences.zh: 后雅有識度，帝每有所為，必豫籌畫。

translations.literal: The empress elegantly had insight and measure; whenever the emperor had something to do, she always planned ahead.
translations.idiomatic: She was poised and far-sighted; whatever her husband planned, she anticipated and shaped.

sentences.zh: 魏明帝世，宣帝居上將之重，諸子並有雄才大略。

translations.literal: In Emperor Ming of Wei’s reign, Emperor Xuan occupied the weight of supreme commander; his sons all had heroic talent and broad strategies.
translations.idiomatic: Under Wei Mingdi, Sima Yi commanded the armies while his sons showed ruthless ambition.

sentences.zh: 后知帝非魏之純臣，而后既魏氏之甥，帝深忌之。

translations.literal: The empress knew the emperor was not a pure minister of Wei, yet the empress was moreover a niece of the Wei clan—deeply the emperor suspected her.
translations.idiomatic: She knew Sima Yi was no loyal servant of Wei, yet as a Wei princess by birth she herself drew his deepest suspicion.

sentences.zh: 青龍二年，遂以鴆崩，時年二十四，葬峻平陵。

translations.literal: In the second Qinglong year she then died by poisoned wine, aged twenty-four, buried at Junping tumulus.
translations.idiomatic: In 234 she was poisoned at twenty-four and buried at Junping mausoleum.

sentences.zh: 武帝登阼，初未追崇，弘訓太后每以為言，泰始二年始加號諡。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, at first he did not posthumously honor her; Empress Dowager Hongxun often spoke of it; only in the second Taishi year did he begin adding title and posthumous name.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Wu took the throne he left her unhonored until Empress Dowager Yang at Hongxun repeatedly pressed the matter; only in 266 did he grant posthumous rank and epithet.

translations.literal: The empress had no sons; she bore five daughters.
translations.idiomatic: She had no sons but five daughters.

translations.literal: Empress Yang Jingxian
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang the Revered and Offered

sentences.zh: 景獻羊皇后諱徽瑜，泰山南城人。

translations.literal: Empress Yang Jingxian, taboo name Huiyu, was a person of Nancheng in Taishan.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang Jingxian, personal name Huiyu, came from Nancheng in Taishan commandery.

translations.literal: Her father Zhi was governor of Shangdang;
translations.idiomatic: Her father Yang Zhi served as governor of Shangdang;

sentences.zh: 后母陳留蔡氏，漢左中郎將邕之女也。

translations.literal: the empress’s mother was a Cai of Chenliu, daughter of Han’s Left General of the Household Cai Yong.
translations.idiomatic: her mother was a Cai from Chenliu, daughter of the Han court poet Cai Yong.

translations.literal: The empress was clever, keen, and had talent and conduct.
translations.idiomatic: She was quick-witted, talented, and principled.

sentences.zh: 景懷皇后崩，景帝更娶鎮北將軍濮陽吳質女，見黜，復納后，無子。

translations.literal: When Empress Jinghuai died, Emperor Jing further married the daughter of Wu Zhi of Puyang, General Who Guards the North; she was dismissed; he took in the empress again; she had no sons.
translations.idiomatic: After Empress Xiahou died, Emperor Jing married Wu Zhi’s daughter, then divorced her, and took Yang Huiyu back; she bore no sons.

sentences.zh: 武帝受禪，居弘訓宮，號弘訓太后。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu received the abdication, she resided in Hongxun Palace, titled Empress Dowager Hongxun.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu assumed the throne she moved to Hongxun Palace as dowager.

sentences.zh: 泰始九年，追贈蔡氏濟陽縣君，諡曰穆。

translations.literal: In the ninth Taishi year Lady Cai was posthumously endowed as Mistress of Jiyang County, posthumous name Mu.
translations.idiomatic: In 273 her mother was posthumously named Lady of Jiyang with the epithet Mu.

sentences.zh: 咸寧四年，太后崩，時年六十五，祔葬峻平陵。

translations.literal: In the fourth Xianning year the empress dowager died, aged sixty-five, buried by accompaniment at Junping tumulus.
translations.idiomatic: She died in 278 at sixty-five and was interred beside Emperor Jing at Junping.

translations.literal: Empress Wang Wenming
translations.idiomatic: Empress Wang the Cultured and Illustrious

sentences.zh: 文明王皇后諱元姬，東海郯人也。

translations.literal: Empress Wang Wenming, taboo name Yuanji, was a native of Tan in Donghai.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Wang Wenming, personal name Yuanji, came from Tan in Donghai commandery.

translations.literal: Her father Su was Central Commandant of the Army in Wei, Marquis of Lanling.
translations.idiomatic: Her father Wang Su served Wei as Central Commandant and Marquis of Lanling.

sentences.zh: 后年八歲，誦詩論，尤善喪服；

translations.literal: At age eight the empress recited the Odes and Analects and was especially good at mourning garments;
translations.idiomatic: At eight she could recite the Odes and Analects and had mastered the ritual chapters on mourning dress;

sentences.zh: 苟有文義，目所一見，必貫於心。

translations.literal: if there was textual meaning, what her eyes once saw, she must thread through her heart.
translations.idiomatic: whatever text she read once lodged permanently in memory.

sentences.zh: 年九歲，遇母疾，扶侍不捨左右，衣不解帶者久之。

translations.literal: At age nine, encountering her mother’s illness, she attended without leaving her side, not undoing her belt for clothing for a long time.
translations.idiomatic: At nine, when her mother fell ill, she nursed her night and day without loosening her sash for weeks.

sentences.zh: 每先意候指，動中所適，由是父母令攝家事，每盡其理。

translations.literal: Always anticipating intention and watching for hints, her actions hit what was fitting; therefore her parents ordered her to manage household affairs, and she always exhausted reason in them.
translations.idiomatic: She anticipated every wish so deftly that her parents put her in charge of the household, which she ran flawlessly.

sentences.zh: 祖朗甚愛異之，曰：「興吾家者，必此女也，惜不為男矣！

translations.literal: Her grandfather Lang greatly loved and regarded her as unusual, saying: “The one who will raise our house must be this girl—alas that she is not a boy!
translations.idiomatic: Her grandfather Wang Lang doted on her, saying, “This girl will redeem our line—if only she were a son!”

sentences.zh: 」年十二，朗薨，后哀戚哭泣，發于自然，其父益加敬異。

translations.literal: ” At twelve Lang died; the empress mourned and wept in grief, arising from the natural; her father increasingly respected her as unusual.
translations.idiomatic: ” When Wang Lang died she was twelve; her grief was utterly spontaneous, and her father prized her even more.

sentences.zh: 既笄，歸于文帝，生武帝及遼東悼王定國、齊獻王攸、城陽哀王兆、廣漢殤王廣德、京兆公主。

translations.literal: After capping-age she married Emperor Wen and bore Emperor Wu, Prince Dingguo of Liaodong, Prince You of Qi, Prince Zhao of Chengyang, Prince Guangde of Guanghan, and the Princess of Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: After coming of age she married Sima Zhao (later Emperor Wen) and bore Sima Yan (Emperor Wu), Princes Dingguo, You, Zhao, and Guangde, and the Princess of Jingzhao.

sentences.zh: 后事舅姑盡婦道，謙沖接下，嬪御有序。

translations.literal: The empress served parents-in-law exhausting wife’s way, humble and yielding in receiving those below, concubines and attendants having order.
translations.idiomatic: She observed every duty to her in-laws, treated inferiors with modesty, and kept the inner household in harmony.

sentences.zh: 及居父喪，身不勝衣，言與淚俱。

translations.literal: When dwelling in mourning for her father, her body did not fill out her garments; speech and tears together.
translations.idiomatic: During her father’s mourning she wasted to skin and bone; every word came with tears.

sentences.zh: 時鍾會以才能見任，后每言于帝曰：「會見利忘義，好為事端，寵過必亂，不可大任。

translations.literal: At the time Zhong Hui was employed for talent and ability; the empress often said to the emperor: “Hui sees profit and forgets righteousness, likes to make incidents; favor passed must bring chaos—he cannot be greatly entrusted.
translations.idiomatic: Zhong Hui had won power through sheer ability; she often warned Emperor Wen, “Zhong chases profit, courts trouble, and will rebel if favor grows—do not give him real authority.”

translations.literal: ” Hui afterward indeed rebelled.
translations.idiomatic: ” Zhong Hui later rose in rebellion, just as she foretold.

sentences.zh: 武帝受禪，尊為皇太后，宮曰崇化。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu received the abdication, she was honored as empress dowager; the palace was called Chonghua.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu took the throne she became empress dowager, with residence in Chonghua Palace.

sentences.zh: 初置宮卿，重選其職，以太常諸葛緒為衛尉，太僕劉原為太僕，宗正曹楷為少府。

translations.literal: At first palace ministers were installed; their offices were heavily selected—Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhuge Xu as Commandant of the Guard, Grand Coachman Liu Yuan as Grand Coachman, Director of the Imperial Clan Cao Kai as Privy Treasurer.
translations.idiomatic: She established palace ministries with careful appointments: Zhuge Xu as minister of the guard, Liu Yuan as grand coachman, Cao Kai as privy treasurer.

sentences.zh: 后雖處尊位，不忘素業，躬執紡績，器服無文，御浣濯之衣，食不參味。

translations.literal: Although the empress occupied an honored position, she did not forget her plain work; personally she held spinning and weaving; vessels and garments had no pattern; she employed washed clothing; food did not mix flavors.
translations.idiomatic: Though dowager, she still spun and wove, wore undyed cloth and laundered robes, and took simple meals without mixed dishes.

sentences.zh: 而敦睦九族，垂心萬物，言必典禮，浸潤不行。

translations.literal: Yet she treated the nine kindreds warmly, let her heart hang over all things; speech always followed canon and ritual; seeping influence did not proceed.
translations.idiomatic: She cherished every branch of kin, cared for all living things, spoke only in classical idiom, and never let private bias seep into policy.

sentences.zh: 帝以后母羊氏未崇諡號，泰始三年下詔曰：「昔漢文追崇靈文之號，武、宣有平原、博平之封，咸所以奉尊尊之敬，廣親親之恩也。

translations.literal: The emperor because the empress’s mother the Yang clan had not been honored with posthumous title, in the third Taishi year issued an edict saying: “Formerly Han Wen posthumously elevated the title of Lingwen; Wu and Xuan had enfeoffments of Pingyuan and Boping—all were means to serve respect to the honored and widen kindness to kin.
translations.idiomatic: Because his mother-in-law lacked posthumous honors, Emperor Wu issued in 267 an edict: “Han Wendi raised Empress Dowager Bo’s title; later Han rulers enfeoffed mothers from Pingyuan and Boping—such acts honor parents and widen kinship grace.”

sentences.zh: 故衛將軍、蘭陵景侯夫人羊氏，含章體順，仁德醇備，內承世冑，出嬪大國，三從之行，率禮無違。

translations.literal: Therefore Lady Yang, wife of General Who Guards the Army, Marquis Jing of Lanling, contained pattern and embodied compliance; humane virtue pure and complete; inwardly inheriting generations of lineage, outwardly marrying a great state; in the conduct of the three followings, leading ritual without violation.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Yang, widow of General Wang Su, Marquis Jing of Lanling, bore inward grace and outward modesty, fulfilled every womanly virtue, linked great houses by marriage, and observed the three obediences without fault.

sentences.zh: 仍遭不造，頻喪統嗣，撫育眾胤，克成家道。

translations.literal: Yet she encountered ill fortune, repeatedly losing heirs who would succeed, fostering many descendants, able to complete family way.
translations.idiomatic: Though Heaven denied her sons and struck down heirs again and again, she raised the wider family and preserved the household.

sentences.zh: 母儀之教，光于邦族，誕啟聖明，祚流萬國。

translations.literal: Motherly model instruction shone on state and clan; she broadly opened sagely brightness; fortune flowed to myriad states.
translations.idiomatic: Her maternal example illuminated kin and state, opened the way for the sage-sovereign, and spread blessing across every realm.

translations.literal: Yet she died young and fell, not encountering fine favor.
translations.idiomatic: Yet she died young before receiving such honors.

sentences.zh: 皇太后孝思蒸蒸，永慕罔極。

translations.literal: The empress dowager’s filial thoughts steam upward; forever longing without limit.
translations.idiomatic: The empress dowager mourns her mother with boundless filial love.

translations.literal: I am moved to preserve surviving instructions; tracing the distant, injuring the breast.
translations.idiomatic: Remembering her teaching, I ache when paying tribute to the past.

sentences.zh: 其封夫人為縣君，依德紀諡，主者詳如舊典。

translations.literal: Let the lady be enfeoffed as county mistress; according to virtue record posthumous name; those in charge detail according to old canons.
translations.idiomatic: Enfeoff her as a county mistress, grant an epithet suited to her virtue, and let the ministry follow precedent.

sentences.zh: 」於是使使持節謁者何融追諡為平陽靖君。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon envoy bearing staff and insignia, Yeoman He Rong posthumously titled her Pingyang Lady Jing.
translations.idiomatic: Envoy He Rong was therefore dispatched with tally and staff to confer posthumously the title Lady Jing of Pingyang.

sentences.zh: 四年，后崩，時年五十二，合葬崇陽陵。

translations.literal: In the fourth year the empress died. She was fifty-two at death and was buried jointly at Chongyang Mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth year she died at fifty-two and was laid beside him in Chongyang Mausoleum.

sentences.zh: 將遷祔，帝手疏后德行，命史官為哀策曰：

translations.literal: When she was to be moved for joint burial, the emperor personally drafted an account of her conduct and ordered the historiographers to compose a dirge of lament, saying:
translations.idiomatic: When her cortège was readied for burial at his side, he drafted her virtues in his own hand and told the historiographers to write a lament—thus:

translations.literal: O clear-bright late queen, you raised our Jin way.
translations.idiomatic: Radiant queen who went before, you lifted high our Jin house.

translations.literal: Your radiant pattern and virtuous fame aided our august father.
translations.idiomatic: Your shining virtue and gracious name steadied our royal father.

translations.literal: Advancing virtue, spreading counsel—you fashioned the great enterprise.
translations.idiomatic: You advanced virtue and wise counsel and helped forge the great enterprise.

translations.literal: You left blessing to the orphaned child; you guarded hall and rafters.
translations.idiomatic: You left blessing to a fatherless heir and preserved the house he would inherit.

translations.literal: We hoped still to lean on your backward glance and forever enjoy agelessness.
translations.idiomatic: We hoped still for your shelter and the gift of your undying care.

translations.literal: Suddenly you ascended far—why did you leave us so soon!
translations.idiomatic: Suddenly you journeyed on—why abandon us this soon!

translations.literal: Deep grief with nowhere to speak—what shall I say to vast Heaven?
translations.idiomatic: Grief too deep for words—how shall I cry to boundless Heaven?

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

translations.literal: From the first birth of the people, they planted kindness and health.
translations.idiomatic: From life’s first dawn kind nurture has sustained the folk.

translations.literal: The emperor chose bright virtue, watching over our late sovereign.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven chose a luminous lady to watch beside our late king.

translations.literal: Heaven set up his mate; our sovereign was illumined.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven set her at his side and glorified our throne.

translations.literal: She founded the state and formed the pair; her virtuous fame knows no bound.
translations.idiomatic: She matched him as co-ruler; her fair fame knows no shore.

translations.literal: Pity me unsuccored—Heaven sternly sends calamity.
translations.idiomatic: Pity your orphaned son—Heaven heaps fresh grief upon him.

translations.literal: The sun set in Mingyi’s darkness; mid-years brought collapse.
translations.idiomatic: The sun dipped into night; in mid-life she was torn away.

translations.literal: Alone in affliction, forever cherishing, crushed and wounded.
translations.idiomatic: I stand alone in mourning, heartsick without healing.

translations.literal: Tracing her lofty way—ah, majestic without end.
translations.idiomatic: When I trace her shining conduct, its grandeur knows no end.

translations.literal: Sea and Mount Tai sent down spirits; generations bore thick blessings.
translations.idiomatic: Sea and Taishan lent her spirit; age after age received rich blessing.

translations.literal: Forever grant heirs and fortune; earnestly was born the cultured mother.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven blessed our line with heirs and gave us a mother steeped in pattern.

translations.literal: Born to receive pure harmony, modest and careful in bearing.
translations.idiomatic: She bore pure harmony in her blood and moved with modest grace.

translations.literal: Honest and straight, she did not waver; she embodied filial piety and brotherly duty.
translations.idiomatic: Her honesty never wavered; she lived filial love and gentle kindness.

translations.literal: The Odes and Documents were her delight; ritual canons were her rule.
translations.idiomatic: She delighted in the classics and held the ritual texts as her compass.

translations.literal: The three obediences without fault; the inner kitchen truly ordered.
translations.idiomatic: She kept the three obediences flawlessly and ordered the inner household aright.

translations.literal: Tracing the late queens, toil and humility are esteemed.
translations.idiomatic: Remembering queens past, she prized humble service above all.

translations.literal: When first in the maiden chamber, she exhausted strength to nurture parents.
translations.idiomatic: In her girlhood she strained every nerve to care for her parents.

translations.literal: She married into a great state and aided the royal foundation.
translations.idiomatic: She married into a great house and steadied the throne’s foundation.

translations.literal: Quiet peace elevated transformation; the imperial enterprise was thereby founded.
translations.idiomatic: Her quiet grace lifted the realm and gave the dynasty its start.

translations.literal: Within she ordered the concubines; without she harmonized the hopes of the age.
translations.idiomatic: Within she schooled the harem; without she answered the hopes of the age.

translations.literal: Treading faith and dwelling in compliance, virtue and conduct flowed smoothly.
translations.idiomatic: Faithful in word and compliant in station, her virtue suffused every quarter.

translations.literal: Diligent without negligence, toilsome yet yielding.
translations.idiomatic: She labored without slack and strove with yielding grace.

translations.literal: Esteeming thrift and restraining splendor, she took simplicity as her model.
translations.idiomatic: She honored plain cloth over display and made simplicity her fashion.

translations.literal: Although she enjoyed loftiness, joy and feasting were not yet tasted.
translations.idiomatic: Though raised to the heights, she never tasted idle revelry.

translations.literal: How could she leave us—whom shall I look up to?
translations.idiomatic: How could she leave us—where shall I lift my eyes?

translations.literal: Alas for my ill fortune—great punishments crowd upon me.
translations.idiomatic: Alas for my ill star—Heaven’s blows strike again and again.

translations.literal: Imperial father turned his back on the world—barely three years have passed.
translations.idiomatic: My royal father left this world hardly three years ago.

translations.literal: Looking up I served my loving mother, hoping for no later hardship.
translations.idiomatic: I leaned on a loving mother and prayed no further grief would come.

translations.literal: Fierce disasters gather still—what crime against Heaven is this?
translations.idiomatic: Yet calamity returns—what sin have I committed against Heaven?

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

translations.literal: The hearse was harnessed at dawn; farewell rites were set within the inner gate.
translations.idiomatic: At dawn the hearse stood ready; parting rites filled the inner court.

translations.literal: The burial wagon’s hubs rolled on—gone, never to pursue.
translations.idiomatic: The jeweled hearse rolled forward—what is gone cannot be reclaimed.

translations.literal: Mournful royal mother—forever sunk beneath spiritual radiance.
translations.idiomatic: Royal mother most dear—your holy light is hid forever.

translations.literal: I advance to cling to the catalpa coffin, looking back to grasp the white banner.
translations.idiomatic: I cling to your catalpa bier and clutch the mourning pennants as I climb.

translations.literal: Trembling in utmost pain—whom shall I tell, on whom rely?
translations.idiomatic: I tremble with pain—whom can I tell, where find shelter?

translations.literal: I pour out feeling and present this document to ease wounded grief.
translations.idiomatic: I pour my heart into this text to ease the ache that breaks me.

translations.literal: Perhaps you still may hear—look upon me, orphaned and left behind.
translations.idiomatic: Perhaps you still may hear—turn once to your forsaken child.

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

sentences.zh: 其後帝追慕不已，復下詔曰：「外曾祖母故司徒王朗夫人楊氏，舅氏尊屬，鄭、劉二從母，先后至愛。

translations.literal: Afterward the emperor’s longing did not cease; he again issued an edict saying: “My maternal great-grandmother, Lady Yang, wife of former Minister of Education Wang Lang, my uncles’ honored kin, and my two maternal aunts of the Zheng and Liu clans were deeply beloved by the late consorts.
translations.idiomatic: Still grieving, he issued another edict: “Lady Yang, wife of former Minister Wang Lang and my maternal great-grandmother, together with my maternal uncles and my two aunts on the Zheng and Liu sides, were cherished by successive empresses.

sentences.zh: 每惟聖善，敦睦遺旨，渭陽之感，永懷靡及。

translations.literal: Whenever pondering their sacred goodness and generous instructions, the Wei-yang longing—forever cherished yet never attained.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I recall their kindness and the generous instructions they left, the ache of a nephew for his mother’s kin stays with me yet can never be satisfied.

sentences.zh: 其封楊夫人及從母為鄉君，邑各五百戶。

translations.literal: Let Lady Yang and the maternal aunts be enfeoffed as village mistresses, five hundred households each.
translations.idiomatic: Let Lady Yang and my maternal aunts each receive the title of village mistress with five hundred taxable households.

sentences.zh: 」太康七年，追贈繼祖母夏侯氏為滎陽鄉君。

translations.literal: ” In the seventh year of Taikang, his step-grandmother Lady Xiahou was posthumously endowed as village mistress of Xingyang.
translations.idiomatic: ” In 286 he posthumously named his step-grandmother Lady Xiahou village mistress of Xingyang.

translations.literal: Empress Yang Wuyuan
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang the Martial and Primordial

sentences.zh: 武元楊皇后諱艷，字瓊芝，弘農華陰人也。

translations.literal: Empress Yang Wuyuan, taboo name Yan, courtesy name Qiongzhi, was a native of Huayin in Hongnong.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang Wuyuan, personal name Yan, courtesy Qiongzhi, came from Huayin in Hongnong commandery.

translations.literal: Her father Wenzhong [2]—see the “Treatise on Outer Kin”;
translations.idiomatic: Her father Yang Wenzhong [2] is treated in the “Treatise on Outer Kin”;

translations.literal: her mother was a Zhao of Tianshui; she died early.
translations.idiomatic: her mother, a Zhao from Tianshui, died while Yang Yan was still young.

sentences.zh: 后依舅家，舅妻仁愛，親乳養后，遣他人乳其子。

translations.literal: The empress relied on her uncle’s household; her uncle’s wife was benevolent and loving, personally suckled and raised the empress, and sent another woman to nurse her own child.
translations.idiomatic: She grew up in her uncle’s house; his wife nursed Yang Yan herself and hired another wet nurse for her own baby.

sentences.zh: 及長，又隨後母段氏，依其家。

translations.literal: When grown, she again followed her stepmother Lady Duan and relied on that household.
translations.idiomatic: Later she lived under her stepmother Lady Duan’s roof.

sentences.zh: 帝以皇太子不堪奉大統，密以語后。

translations.literal: The emperor considered the crown prince unable to uphold the great line and secretly spoke of it to the empress.
translations.idiomatic: Believing the crown prince unfit to inherit the realm, he confided as much privately to the empress.

sentences.zh: 后曰：「立嫡以長不以賢，豈可動乎？

translations.literal: The empress said: “Establishing the heir depends on seniority among legitimate sons, not on talent—how can that be altered?
translations.idiomatic: She replied, “The eldest legitimate son succeeds regardless of talent—how can we undo that?”

sentences.zh: 」初，賈充妻郭氏使賂后，求以女為太子妃。

translations.literal: ” At first Jia Chong’s wife Lady Guo sent bribes to the empress, seeking to make her daughter crown princess.
translations.idiomatic: ” Earlier Jia Chong’s wife Lady Guo had bribed her to secure her daughter as crown princess.

sentences.zh: 及議太子婚，帝欲娶衛瓘女。

translations.literal: When discussing the crown prince’s marriage, the emperor wished to take Wei Guan’s daughter.
translations.idiomatic: When the heir’s marriage came under debate, the emperor favored Wei Guan’s daughter.

sentences.zh: 然后盛稱賈后有淑德，又密使太子太傅荀顗進言，上乃聽之。

translations.literal: But the empress greatly praised Consort Jia’s virtuous conduct, and also secretly had Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince Xun Yi speak; the sovereign then consented.
translations.idiomatic: The empress loudly praised Lady Jia’s virtue and secretly had Grand Tutor Xun Yi speak for her, so the emperor yielded.

sentences.zh: 泰始中，帝博選良家以充後宮，先下書禁天下嫁娶，使宦者乘使車，給騶騎，馳傳州郡，召充選者使后揀擇。

translations.literal: In the Taishi era the emperor broadly selected good families to fill the rear palace; first he issued a document forbidding marriage in the realm, had eunuchs ride dispatch coaches provided with outriders, gallop relay orders to provinces and commanderies, summon those filling selection and had the empress pick and choose.
translations.idiomatic: Midway through Taishi he cast a wide net for palace women, banned commoners from marrying, sent eunuchs in official carriages with escorts racing along post roads to every commandery, and had the candidates presented to the empress for her verdict.

sentences.zh: 后性妒，惟取潔白長大，其端正美麗者並不見留。

translations.literal: The empress was by nature jealous; she only took those fair and tall; those properly beautiful were none of them retained.
translations.idiomatic: Jealous by nature, she kept only plain, towering girls and rejected every truly lovely face.

sentences.zh: 時卞藩女有美色，帝掩扇謂后曰：「卞氏女佳。

translations.literal: At the time Bian Fan’s daughter had beautiful looks; the emperor hid behind a fan and said to the empress: “Bian’s daughter is excellent.
translations.idiomatic: When Bian Fan’s daughter proved breathtaking, the emperor hid behind his fan and said, “The Bian girl is a jewel.

sentences.zh: 」后曰：「藩三世后族，其女不可枉以卑位。

translations.literal: ” The empress said: “The Bian clan for three generations has been empress kin—their daughter cannot be slighted with low rank.
translations.idiomatic: ” The empress answered, “Three generations of Bians have supplied empresses—such a bride cannot be parked in a petty title.

translations.literal: ” The emperor then stopped.
translations.idiomatic: ” He dropped the matter.

sentences.zh: 司徒李胤、鎮軍大將軍胡奮、廷尉諸葛沖、太僕臧權、侍中馮蓀、秘書郎左思及世族子女並充三夫人九嬪之列。

translations.literal: Minister of Education Li Yin, General Who Guards the Army Hu Fen, Commandant of Justice Zhuge Chong, Grand Coachman Zang Quan, Palace Attendant Feng Sun, Secretary Court Gentleman Zuo Si, and daughters of eminent clans together filled the ranks of three ladies and nine bin.
translations.idiomatic: The daughters of Li Yin, Hu Fen, Zhuge Chong, Zang Quan, Feng Sun, Zuo Si, and other great houses were placed among the Three Ladies and the Nine Concubines.

sentences.zh: 司、冀、兗、豫四州二千石將吏家，補良人以下。

translations.literal: Families of two-thousand-shi commandery officials in Si, Ji, Yan, and Yu four prefectures supplied ranks below liangren.
translations.idiomatic: From Si, Ji, Yan, and Yu the daughters of prefects and local officers filled the ranks below Good Woman.

sentences.zh: 名家盛族子女，多敗衣瘁貌以避之。

translations.literal: Sons and daughters of famous houses and great clans mostly wore tattered clothes and haggard looks to avoid it.
translations.idiomatic: Great families dressed their girls in rags and smeared their faces to dodge the draft.

sentences.zh: 及后有疾，見帝素幸胡夫人，恐後立之，慮太子不安。

translations.literal: When the empress had illness, she saw the emperor always favored Lady Hu and feared she would later be established, worrying for the crown prince’s security.
translations.idiomatic: When she fell ill and saw how he favored Lady Hu, she feared a future empress would threaten her son.

sentences.zh: 臨終，枕帝膝曰：「叔父駿女男胤有德色，願陛下以備六宮。

translations.literal: At the end, pillowing on the emperor’s knee she said: “Uncle Yang Jun’s niece has virtue and beauty; I beg Your Majesty to keep her for the six palaces.
translations.idiomatic: Dying with her head on his knee she said, “Your uncle Yang Jun’s niece combines virtue and beauty—please bring her into the six palaces.

translations.literal: ” Thereupon she wept sadly; the emperor promised with flowing tears.
translations.idiomatic: ” She wept; he swore through tears to comply.

sentences.zh: 泰始十年，崩於明光殿，絕于帝膝，時年三十七。

translations.literal: In the tenth Taishi year she died in Mingguang Hall, expired on the emperor’s knee, aged thirty-seven.
translations.idiomatic: She died in 274 in Mingguang Hall on his lap, thirty-seven years old.

sentences.zh: 詔曰：「皇后逮事先后，常冀能終始永奉宗廟，一旦殂隕，痛悼傷懷。

translations.literal: An edict said: “The empress served the late consorts in succession, always hoping to be able from beginning to end forever to serve the ancestral temple; suddenly she has fallen—pain and grief wound the heart.
translations.idiomatic: The edict read, “The empress served my late mothers and hoped to honor the shrines to the end; her sudden death tears my heart.

sentences.zh: 每自以夙喪二親，於家門之情特隆。

translations.literal: She often because early lost both parents, toward household affection was especially strong.
translations.idiomatic: Orphaned young, she cherished family ties above all else.

sentences.zh: 又有心欲改葬父祖，以頃者務崇儉約，初不有言，近垂困，說此意，情亦愍之。

translations.literal: Also she had in mind wishing to reburial father and grandparents; because recent affairs strove to esteem thrift, at first she did not speak; drawing near to death’s agony she stated this intent—the feeling also pities her.
translations.idiomatic: She longed to move her parents’ graves but, while court fashion prized austerity, stayed silent until her final hours—this wish moves us still.

sentences.zh: 其使領前軍將軍駿等自克改葬之宜，至時，主者供給葬事。

translations.literal: Let General of the Van Yang Jun and others themselves determine the propriety of reburial; when the time comes, those in charge shall supply burial affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Let Forward-General Yang Jun and his colleagues arrange the reburials; officials shall supply whatever is needed when the day comes.

sentences.zh: 賜諡母趙氏為縣君，以繼母段氏為鄉君。

translations.literal: Posthumously grant Lady Zhao mother title as county mistress, and stepmother Lady Duan as village mistress.
translations.idiomatic: Honor her mother Lady Zhao as county mistress and her stepmother Lady Duan as village mistress.

sentences.zh: 傳不云乎，『慎終追遠，民德歸厚』。

translations.literal: Does not the tradition say, ‘Being careful in one’s end and remembering the remote makes the people’s virtue thick’?
translations.idiomatic: Has not the classic said, ‘Care for the dead and honor the past, and the people grow in virtue’?

sentences.zh: 且使亡者有知，尚或嘉之。」

translations.literal: Moreover, if the dead have knowledge, perhaps they will approve.”
translations.idiomatic: Should the dead still know anything of us, they may rejoice in this kindness.”

sentences.zh: 于是有司卜吉，窀穸有期，乃命史臣作哀策敘懷。

translations.literal: Thereupon the officials divined an auspicious day; the burial had a set time; then he ordered the scribes to compose a dirge narrating feeling.
translations.idiomatic: Officers chose an auspicious day for interment and scribes were told to write a lament.

translations.literal: The words say:
translations.idiomatic: It reads:

translations.literal: Heaven and earth match in sequence; they accomplish transformation of the two modes.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth keep their stations and shape the yin and yang spheres.

translations.literal: The king comes to have a household; the way lies in husband and wife.
translations.idiomatic: The king wins a true household because husband and wife uphold the Way.

translations.literal: Jiang Yuan aided Ku; two consorts raised Gui.
translations.idiomatic: Jiang Yuan aided Emperor Ku; the two brides raised the house of Gui.

translations.literal: Looking up I hope in ancient past; I hope likewise same norm.
translations.idiomatic: We look to antiquity and pray our norm matches theirs.

translations.literal: Now why is it not so—the bright mandate early deficient?
translations.idiomatic: Why are we denied that grace—why was her bright mandate cut short?

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

translations.literal: I respond to charts and tallies, overseeing the myriad regions.
translations.idiomatic: I hold the celestial charts and rule the myriad lands.

translations.literal: Correct position lies within; truly it lies in the consorts.
translations.idiomatic: The inner court’s order rests with its ladies.

translations.literal: Heaven made the match; splendidly arose auspice.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven forged our match and sent forth splendid omens.

translations.literal: Rivers and peaks sent down spirits; they opened fortune at Huayang.
translations.idiomatic: River and peak lent her spirit and opened blessing in Huayang.

translations.literal: Generation after generation abundant spread; vermillion cords thus shine.
translations.idiomatic: Generation on generation flourished; vermillion seals blaze forth.

translations.literal: Continue the woman’s conduct; receive mandate broadly to assist.
translations.idiomatic: She renewed womanly duty and answered Heaven’s wide charge.

translations.literal: Come to wing the state and house; statute and measure are the constant.
translations.idiomatic: She came to shield house and realm and held fast to every norm.

translations.literal: Brighten women’s instruction; virtue’s fame is displayed.
translations.idiomatic: She brightened women’s teaching and her fair fame rang wide.

translations.literal: Formerly my late mother—brilliant glorious auspicious light.
translations.idiomatic: My late mother shone with auspicious light.

translations.literal: The empress received former instruction; she upheld and narrated remaining fragrance.
translations.idiomatic: This empress followed her teaching and kept her fragrance alive.

translations.literal: Should continue fine reputation; continue the sequence without waste.
translations.idiomatic: She should have prolonged that sweet renown and kept our line from wandering astray.

translations.literal: How can we not mourn—she turned her back on the age and collapsed.
translations.idiomatic: Why should Heaven not pity her—she left the living world too soon.

translations.literal: Gazing toward Qi she has no lord; forever gone are winter and summer sacrifices.
translations.idiomatic: Ancestral feasts in Qi lack their host; steam offerings rise without her.

translations.literal: Tracing remembrance brings endless mourning; across the soil every heart breaks.
translations.idiomatic: Memory cuts deep; the whole realm shares this wound.

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

translations.literal: The tumulus ground already narrowed; she will move to the silent capital.
translations.idiomatic: The vault is closed; her shades depart for darkness.

translations.literal: At midnight they harness at dawn; the chief consort journeys hence.
translations.idiomatic: Torches at midnight, dawn departure—the queen sets forth.

translations.literal: The palace gates fall mute; steps and courts stand empty.
translations.idiomatic: The inner halls fall silent; courtyard stairs lie bare.

translations.literal: They set the farewell rites, spread the mourning sash, announce the coach and open the road.
translations.idiomatic: Bearers array cords of parting, proclaim the hearse, and clear the way.

translations.literal: She wears kingfisher robe and barren-rabbit cloak; her likeness rides the draped coach.
translations.idiomatic: Kingfisher seams and pheasant gown ride with her image on the draped bier.

translations.literal: The golden carriage dimly veils; skirts and curtains do not spread.
translations.idiomatic: Gold carriage lamps flicker; pall curtains stay furled in grief.

translations.literal: A thousand carriages stir their hubs; six chestnuts paw and linger.
translations.idiomatic: Countless wheels roll; six bays champ at their traces.

translations.literal: The inscribed banner marks the way; feather screens sweep cloud-like.
translations.idiomatic: Spirit pennons lift high; plumed shades drift like clouds.

translations.literal: So many share one road; awed mourners throng on foot.
translations.idiomatic: All realms march together; the funeral train towers sheer.

translations.literal: Who fails to cherish her—ten thousand hearts ache at once.
translations.idiomatic: Who could withhold tears—a myriad souls ache together.

translations.literal: Calm her spirit with Yu’s divination; lay her body to rest in the dark lodge.
translations.idiomatic: Give her peace per oracle rites; settle her in the earthen vault.

translations.literal: Earthen chamber and pottery vessels match the plain rules of her first estate.
translations.idiomatic: Clay chamber and pottery jars restore the humble pattern from her youth.

translations.literal: Align deed with posthumous title; her fame reaches all eight quarters.
translations.idiomatic: Virtue frames her epithet; her name crosses every quarter.

translations.literal: Though she leaves Mingguang’s light, she joins her royal mother-in-law.
translations.idiomatic: Though she leaves the sunny halls, she rests beside her queenly ancestress.

translations.literal: She sinks yet does not decay—worldly virtue becomes model for ages.
translations.idiomatic: Death cannot dissolve her—her house’s virtue turns scripture.

translations.literal: Alas, oh grief!
translations.idiomatic: Alas for this sorrow!

translations.literal: She was buried at Junyang Mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: They laid her to rest at Junyang.

translations.literal: Empress Yang Wudao
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang the Martial and Mourned

sentences.zh: 武悼楊皇后諱芷，字季蘭，小字男胤，元后從妹。

translations.literal: Empress Yang Wudao, taboo name Zhi, courtesy name Jilan, childhood name Nanyin, was a younger cousin of Empress Yuan.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Yang Wudao—personal name Zhi, courtesy Jilan, pet name Nanyin—was cousin to the founding empress.

translations.literal: Her father Jun has a separate biography.
translations.idiomatic: Her father Yang Jun has his own biography.

translations.literal: In the second Xianning year she was established as empress.
translations.idiomatic: She became empress in 276.

sentences.zh: 婉嫕有婦德，美映椒房，甚有寵。

translations.literal: Gracious and yielding, she possessed womanly virtue; her beauty lit the pepper chambers and she enjoyed deep favor.
translations.idiomatic: Gentle and virtuous, she brightened the harem and won enduring favor.

sentences.zh: 生渤海殤王，早薨，遂無子。

translations.literal: She bore Prince Huaihai of Bohai, who died young; thereafter she had no sons.
translations.idiomatic: Her son the prince of Bohai died in infancy, leaving her without heirs.

sentences.zh: 太康九年，后率內外夫人命婦躬桑于西郊，賜帛各有差。

translations.literal: In the ninth Taikang year the empress led palace ladies and titled wives to tend silkworms at the western suburb and granted silk in graded amounts.
translations.idiomatic: In 288 she led court ladies to the western suburban silkworm rite and dispensed silk rewards by rank.

sentences.zh: 太子妃賈氏妒忌，帝將廢之。

translations.literal: Crown Princess Jia was jealous; the emperor was about to depose her.
translations.idiomatic: Jealous Crown Princess Jia faced deposition.

sentences.zh: 后言於帝曰：「賈公閭有勳社稷，猶當數世宥之。

translations.literal: The empress said to the emperor: “Lord Jia has merit for state—his house deserves indulgence for generations.
translations.idiomatic: She urged him, “Jia Chong secured the dynasty—his clan merits lasting grace.

sentences.zh: 賈妃親是其女，正復妒忌之間，不足以一眚掩其大德。

translations.literal: The Jia consort is his own daughter; amid jealousy alone, one blemish cannot veil his great virtue.
translations.idiomatic: His daughter is princess—in mere spite one flaw cannot bury his great merit.

sentences.zh: 」后又數誡厲妃，妃不知后之助己，因以致恨，謂后構之於帝，忿怨彌深。

translations.literal: ” Later she repeatedly warned and rebuked the princess; the princess did not realize the empress aided her and therefore bore hatred, believing the empress framed her before the emperor—resentment grew deeper.
translations.idiomatic: She later scolded the princess repeatedly; blind to this help, Jia Nanfeng blamed her for slander and hated her all the more.

translations.literal: When the emperor died, she was honored as empress dowager.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Wu died she became empress dowager.

sentences.zh: 賈后凶悖，忌后父駿執權，遂誣駿為亂，使楚王瑋與東安王繇稱詔誅駿。

translations.literal: Empress Jia was vicious; she resented her father Jun holding power, then slandered Jun as rebellious and had Prince Chu Wei and Prince Dongan Yao forge edicts to execute Jun.
translations.idiomatic: Vicious Jia Nanfeng feared Yang Jun; she accused him of treason and had Sima Wei and Sima Yao murder him with forged orders.

sentences.zh: 內外隔塞，后題帛為書，射之城外，曰「救太傅者有賞」，賈后因宣言太后同逆。

translations.literal: Inner and outer courts were blocked; the empress wrote on silk, shot it beyond the walls, saying “Whoever rescues the grand tutor will be rewarded”; Empress Jia then declared the dowager abetted treason.
translations.idiomatic: Cut off from aid, she shot silk pleas over the wall offering reward to save Yang Jun; Jia then claimed the dowager joined the plot.

sentences.zh: 駿既死，詔使後軍將軍荀悝送后于永寧宮。

translations.literal: After Jun died, an edict ordered Rear-General Xun Kui to escort the empress to Yongning Palace.
translations.idiomatic: After Yang Jun fell, Rear-General Xun Kui was ordered to move her to Yongning Palace.

sentences.zh: 特全后母高都君龐氏之命，聽就后居止。

translations.literal: Her mother Lady Pang of Gaodu Commandery was specially spared and allowed to stay with the dowager.
translations.idiomatic: Her mother Lady Pang was spared and permitted to live with her.

sentences.zh: 賈后諷群公有司奏曰：「皇太后陰漸姦謀，圖危社稷，飛箭繫書，要募將士，同惡相濟，自絕于天。

translations.literal: Empress Jia prompted assembled dukes and offices to memorialize: “The empress dowager secretly carried treason, plotted against the altars, flew arrows with letters tied, summoned soldiers—wicked men aided her and she cut herself off from Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Jia’s faction petitioned: “The dowager schemed treason, imperiled the state, shot letters beyond the walls, and recruited troops—criminals helped her and Heaven abandoned her.

sentences.zh: 魯侯絕文姜，春秋所許，蓋以奉順祖宗，任至公於天下。

translations.literal: Duke Lu cut off Wen Jiang—the Spring and Autumn approves—because one must honor ancestors and hold utmost fairness toward the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Lu cut ties with Wen Jiang, which the Annals condone, to serve ancestors and justice.

sentences.zh: 陛下雖懷無已之情，臣下不敢奉詔。

translations.literal: Although Your Majesty harbors endless feeling, your servants dare not obey the edict.
translations.idiomatic: We know your grief, sire, yet we cannot sanction mercy.

sentences.zh: 可宣敕王公于朝堂會議。

translations.literal: Let an order proclaim that kings and dukes convene in the court hall to deliberate.
translations.idiomatic: Summon princes and ministers to the outer court for debate.

translations.literal: ” An edict said: “This is a great matter—consider it again.
translations.idiomatic: ” The throne replied, “Weighty—deliberate further.

sentences.zh: 」有司又奏：「駿藉外戚之資，居冢宰之任，陛下既居諒闇，委以重權，至乃陰圖凶逆，布樹私黨。

translations.literal: ” The offices again memorialized: “Jun relied on affinal backing and held prime minister’s charge; while Your Majesty mourned in the dark palace he received heavy trust, yet secretly plotted treason and planted private partisans.
translations.idiomatic: ” They answered: “Yang Jun used kinship to seize power; while you mourned he plotted rebellion and packed offices with clients.

sentences.zh: 皇太后內為脣齒，協同逆謀，禍釁既彰，背捍詔命，阻兵負眾，血刃宮省，而復流書募眾，以獎凶黨，上背祖宗之靈，下絕億兆之望。

translations.literal: The empress dowager was his lip and tooth within; she joined the wicked plot. Once the stench showed, she defied decrees, blocked armies, and bloodied the palace—yet still flew letters to recruit crowds and reward villains, betraying ancestors above and cutting off the myriad hopes below.
translations.idiomatic: The dowager abetted him; when crime surfaced she resisted orders, armed her faction, and stained the palace—yet still shot appeals to arm traitors, dishonoring spirits and people.

sentences.zh: 昔文姜與亂，春秋所貶，呂宗叛戾，高后降配，宜廢皇太后為峻陽庶人。

translations.literal: Formerly Wen Jiang joined turmoil—the Spring and Autumn demoted her; the Lü clan rebelled and Empress Gao was lowered in pairing. She should be demoted from empress dowager to commoner of Junyang.
translations.idiomatic: Like Wen Jiang or Empress Lü, she must be struck from dowager rank and made a commoner of Junyang.

sentences.zh: 」中書監張華等以為「太后非得罪于先帝者也，今黨惡所親，[3]為不母于聖世。

translations.literal: ” Palace Supervisor Zhang Hua and others held: “The dowager did not offend the late emperor; now she joins wicked kin—she fails motherhood toward this sage age [3].
translations.idiomatic: ” Zhang Hua argued: “She never wronged Emperor Wu; siding with villains now breaks maternal duty in our era [3].

sentences.zh: 宜依孝成趙皇后故事，曰武帝皇后，處之離宮，以全貴終之恩。

translations.literal: She should follow Empress Zhao of Emperor Cheng’s precedent—styled Empress of Emperor Wu and housed in a detached palace to preserve honored kindness to the end.
translations.idiomatic: Treat her like Chengdi’s Zhao—call her Emperor Wu’s consort, lodge her apart, yet grant a decent end.

sentences.zh: 」尚書令、下邳王晃等議曰：「皇太后與駿潛謀，欲危社稷，不可復奉承宗廟，配合先帝。

translations.literal: ” Minister Director Prince Kang of Xiapi Huan and others debated: “The empress dowager secretly plotted with Jun to overturn the state—she cannot again serve the temple or pair with the late emperor.
translations.idiomatic: ” Wang Huang countered: “She conspired with Yang Jun—she cannot share Wu’s temple.

translations.literal: Her honored title should be stripped and she banished to Metal-Walled Fortress.
translations.idiomatic: Strip her titles and lock her in Jinyong.

sentences.zh: 」于是有司奏：「請從晃等議，廢太后為庶人。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon the offices petitioned: “We ask following Huang’s proposal—depose the dowager as commoner.
translations.idiomatic: ” Officials asked to adopt Huang and reduce her to commoner.

sentences.zh: 遣使者以太牢告于郊廟，以奉承祖宗之命，稱萬國之望。

translations.literal: Dispatch envoys with grand sacrifice to announce at suburban altars and ancestral temple, obeying ancestor spirits and answering myriad lands’ expectation.
translations.idiomatic: Announce it with suburban bull sacrifice to ancestors and satisfy the realm.

sentences.zh: 至於諸所供奉，可順聖恩，務從豐厚。

translations.literal: As for all provisions supplied, follow sagely kindness and strive for abundance.
translations.idiomatic: Let her maintenance stay generous per your mercy.

translations.literal: ” The edict did not permit.
translations.idiomatic: ” The emperor refused.

translations.literal: The offices pressed again; then he consented.
translations.idiomatic: They insisted again; he yielded.

sentences.zh: 又奏：「楊駿造亂，家屬應誅，詔原其妻龐命，以慰太后之心。

translations.literal: They also memorialized: “Yang Jun raised rebellion—his kin deserve execution; the edict spared his wife Pang to console the dowager.
translations.idiomatic: They added: “Yang Jun’s clan should die; you spared Lady Pang to comfort the dowager.

sentences.zh: 今太后廢為庶人，請以龐付廷尉行刑。

translations.literal: Now that the dowager is demoted to commoner, we ask that Pang be handed to the Commandant of Justice for execution.
translations.idiomatic: Now that she is a commoner, execute Lady Pang.

translations.literal: ” The edict said: “Let Pang follow the commoner.
translations.idiomatic: ” He ruled: “Let Lady Pang stay with her.

translations.literal: ” The offices, courting Empress Jia’s intent, pressed firmly; then he followed.
translations.idiomatic: ” Bowing to Jia’s will they insisted until he agreed.

sentences.zh: 龐臨刑，太后抱持號叫，截髮稽顙，上表詣賈后稱妾，請全母命，不見省。

translations.literal: When Pang faced execution, the empress dowager clutched her, wailing; she cut her hair and knocked her forehead, submitted a memorial as concubine to Empress Jia begging to save her mother’s life—she was not granted audience.
translations.idiomatic: At Lady Pang’s execution the dowager clung to her, cut her hair, kowtowed, signed herself Jia’s servant to beg for mercy—Jia ignored her.

sentences.zh: 初，太后尚有侍御十餘人，賈后奪之，絕膳而崩，時年三十四，在位十五年。

translations.literal: At first the dowager still had more than ten attendants; Empress Jia seized them; she starved and died, aged thirty-four, having held rank fifteen years.
translations.idiomatic: Jia stripped her servants; she starved at thirty-four after fifteen years as consort.

sentences.zh: 賈后又信妖巫，謂太后必訴冤先帝，乃覆而殯之，施諸厭劾符書藥物。

translations.literal: Empress Jia further trusted witchcraft, fearing the dowager would appeal her grievance to the late emperor; she therefore buried her face-down with curse charms and drugs.
translations.idiomatic: Jia feared her ghost would accuse Emperor Wu, so she buried her prone under talismans.

sentences.zh: 世祖武皇帝光有四海，元皇后應乾作配。

translations.literal: Shizu Emperor Wu glorified the four seas; his primal empress matched Heaven’s pivot.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu illumined the realm; his first empress answered Heaven.

sentences.zh: 元后既崩，悼后繼作，至楊駿肆逆，禍延天母。

translations.literal: After the primal empress died, the mourned empress succeeded; when Yang Jun ran riot, calamity reached the Mother of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: After Yang Yan died came Yang Zhi; Yang Jun’s treason dragged down the queen mother.

sentences.zh: 孝懷皇帝追復號諡，豈不以鯀殛禹興，義在不替者乎！

translations.literal: Emperor Huai restored her title and epithet—is this not because Gun was executed yet Yu rose—the principle of unbroken obligation?
translations.idiomatic: Huai restored her honors—as Gun fell but Yu rose, duty survives.

sentences.zh: 又太寧二年，臣忝宗正，帝譜泯棄，罔所循按。

translations.literal: Moreover in the second Taining year I humbly served as Director of the Imperial Clan; imperial genealogies were lost—nothing to consult.
translations.idiomatic: In Taining 316 I held the clan office; registers were gone.

sentences.zh: 時博諮舊齒，以定昭穆，與故驃騎將軍華恒、尚書荀崧、侍中荀邃因舊譜參論撰次，尊號之重，一無改替。

translations.literal: We broadly queried elders to fix generations and, with former General of Agile Cavalry Hua Heng, Minister Xun Song, Palace Attendant Xun Sui, reviewed old lists to compile order—her lofty title stayed unchanged.
translations.idiomatic: With Hua Heng, Xun Song, and Xun Sui we recomposed charts—her rank stood firm.

sentences.zh: 今聖上孝思，祗肅禋祀，詢及群司，將以恢定大禮。

translations.literal: Now our sage sovereign’s filial care solemnly tends sacrifice; he asks all bureaus to settle great ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Today’s ruler seeks your counsel to fix court ritual.

sentences.zh: 臣輒思詳，伏見惠皇帝起居注、群臣議奏，列駿作逆謀，危社稷，引魯之文姜，漢之呂后。

translations.literal: I have reflected carefully: in Emperor Hui’s daily records and ministers’ memorials they listed Jun’s treason, imperiling altars, citing Lu’s Wen Jiang and Han’s Empress Lü.
translations.idiomatic: Hui’s archives cite Wen Jiang and Empress Lü against Yang Jun.

sentences.zh: 臣竊以文姜雖莊公之母，實為父讎；

translations.literal: I quietly note that although Wen Jiang was Duke Zhuang’s mother, she was truly her husband’s foe;
translations.idiomatic: Wen Jiang was Duke Huan’s killer despite bearing Zhuang—

sentences.zh: 呂后寵樹私戚，幾危劉氏，按此二事異于今日。

translations.literal: Empress Lü favored kin until she nearly ended the Liu house—these two cases differ from today.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Lü nearly ruined Han—these differ from Yang Zhi.

sentences.zh: 昔漢章帝竇后殺和帝之母，和帝即位盡誅諸竇。

translations.literal: Formerly Dou empress of Han Zhangdi killed Emperor He’s mother; when He ascended he slaughtered the Dou clan.
translations.idiomatic: Zhangdi’s Dou killed He’s mother; He wiped out the Dous.

sentences.zh: 當時議者欲貶竇后，及后之亡，欲不以禮葬。

translations.literal: Debates then wished to demote Dou empress; when she died some wished denial of ritual burial.
translations.idiomatic: Critics then sought to shame Dou and withhold burial rites.

sentences.zh: 和帝以奉事十年，義不可違，臣子之道，務從豐厚，仁明之稱，表于往代。

translations.literal: He had served her ten years—duty forbade cruelty; ministers pursued lavish burial—his humanity shone for ages.
translations.idiomatic: He refused cruelty after ten years’ care—his mercy became legend.

sentences.zh: 又見故尚書僕射裴頠議悼后故事，稱繼母雖出，追服無改。

translations.literal: I also saw former Minister Director Pei Yi’s opinion on Empress Dao’s case—though a stepmother had departed, mourning obligations stayed unchanged.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Yi argued Emperor Ai’s mourned empress kept mourning even after divorce.

sentences.zh: 是以孝懷皇帝尊崇號諡，還葬峻陵。

translations.literal: Therefore Emperor Huai restored honored title and epithet and reburied her at Jun Mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: So Huai restored her posthumous honors at Junling.

sentences.zh: 此則母子道全，而廢事蕩革也。

translations.literal: Thus mother-son duty stayed whole while violent deeds were swept away.
translations.idiomatic: Kin duty survived though politics had fouled them.

sentences.zh: 于時祭于弘訓之宮，未入太廟。

translations.literal: At that time sacrifice occurred at Hongxun Palace—not yet entering the great temple.
translations.idiomatic: She received offerings only at Hongxun, not the grand temple.

sentences.zh: 蓋是事之未盡，非義典也。

translations.literal: That was because the matter was unfinished—not canonical meaning.
translations.idiomatic: That showed work unfinished, not proper liturgy.

sentences.zh: 若以悼后復位為宜，則應配食世祖；

translations.literal: If restoring Empress Dao is right, she should share Emperor Wu’s offerings;
translations.idiomatic: If Yang Zhi deserves restoration, she must join Wu’s temple;

sentences.zh: 若以復之為非，則譜諡宜闕，未有位號居正，而偏祠別室者也。

translations.literal: if restoring her is wrong, then genealogies and epithets should lapse—one cannot hold orthodox rank yet dwell in a side shrine alone.
translations.idiomatic: if not, her titles should lapse—no legitimate rank receives only a side altar.

sentences.zh: 若以孝懷皇帝私隆母子之道，特為立廟者，此苟崇私情，有虧國典，則國譜帝諱，皆宜除棄，匪徒不得同祀于世祖之廟也。

translations.literal: If Emperor Huai privately enlarged mother-son feeling and built a special temple, that would exalt private affection yet wound state canon—then clan registers and temple names should all be discarded, not merely barred from Wu’s temple.
translations.idiomatic: A private shrine for filial piety alone would break precedent and void every register.

sentences.zh: 會稽王昱、中書監庾冰、中書令何充、尚書令諸葛恢、尚書謝廣、光祿勳留擢、丹楊尹殷融、護軍將軍馮懷、散騎常侍鄧逸等咸從潭議，由是太后配食武帝。

translations.literal: Prince Hui of Kuaiji Yu, Palace Supervisor Yu Bing, Palace Director He Chong, Minister Director Zhuge Hui, Minister Xie Guang, Superintendent of the Household Liu Zhuo, Intendant of Danyang Yin Rong, Defender-general Feng Huai, and Palace Rider Deng Yi all followed Tan’s opinion; thereby the dowager shared Emperor Wu’s sacrifices.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Yi, Yu Bing, He Chong, Zhuge Hui, Xie Guang, Liu Zhuo, Yin Rong, Feng Huai, and Deng Yi endorsed Tan—Yang Zhi joined Wu’s temple.

translations.literal: Honorable Lady Zuo
translations.idiomatic: Lady Zuo of Honorable Rank

translations.literal: The honorable lady Zuo was named Fen.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Zuo Fen bore that name.

translations.literal: Her brother Si has a separate biography.
translations.idiomatic: Her brother Zuo Si has his own biography.

sentences.zh: 芬少好學，善綴文，名亞于思，武帝聞而納之。

translations.literal: Fen from youth loved learning, excelled at composing, her fame second only to Si’s; Emperor Wu heard of her and took her in.
translations.idiomatic: A scholar and poet second only to Zuo Si, she entered Emperor Wu’s harem by reputation.

translations.literal: In the eighth Taishi year she was appointed Xiuyi.
translations.idiomatic: In 272 she became Xiuyi.

sentences.zh: 受詔作愁思之文，因為離思賦曰：

translations.literal: Receiving an edict to compose a text on sorrowful longing, she therefore wrote the “Rhapsody on Parting Longing,” saying:
translations.idiomatic: Ordered to write on longing, she penned “Rhapsody on Parting Longing”:

sentences.zh: 生蓬戶之側陋兮，不閑習於文符。

translations.literal: Born beside a ramshackle gate—I never practiced literary tokens.
translations.idiomatic: Raised by a humble gate—I never studied formal genres.

sentences.zh: 不見圖畫之妙像兮，不聞先哲之典謨。

translations.literal: I never saw painted beauties nor heard ancient sages’ counsels.
translations.idiomatic: I never traced gallery portraits nor heard wise exempla.

sentences.zh: 既愚陋而寡識兮，謬忝廁于紫廬。

translations.literal: Dull and ignorant, yet wrongly admitted to the purple lodge.
translations.idiomatic: Crude and shallow, I stumbled into the purple halls.

sentences.zh: 非草苗之所處兮，恒怵惕以憂懼。

translations.literal: No weed seedling belongs here—I tremble ever in dread.
translations.idiomatic: I am grass out of place—I live in constant fear.

sentences.zh: 懷思慕之忉怛兮，兼始終之萬慮。

translations.literal: Cherishing longing’s ache, I bear myriad cares from first to last.
translations.idiomatic: Love and sorrow knot every moment.

sentences.zh: 嗟隱憂之沈積兮，獨鬱結而靡訴。

translations.literal: Alas, hidden grief piles deep—alone I knot inward with nowhere to speak.
translations.idiomatic: Hidden grief heaps high; I choke with words unsaid.

sentences.zh: 意慘憒而無聊兮，思纏綿以增慕。

translations.literal: My heart is bleak and restless; longing winds tighter and deepens love.
translations.idiomatic: My spirit dulls; longing coils tighter.

sentences.zh: 夜耿耿而不寐兮，魂憧憧而至曙。

translations.literal: Night stretches sleepless; my soul wanders until dawn.
translations.idiomatic: Nights are endless; my soul drifts till daylight.

sentences.zh: 風騷騷而四起兮，霜皚皚而依庭。

translations.literal: Wind whistles from every side; frost gleams white along the courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: Wind sighs on four sides; frost lines the yard.

sentences.zh: 日晻曖而無光兮，氣懰慄以洌清。

translations.literal: The sun dims without light; the air bites sharp and clear.
translations.idiomatic: Sunlight fades; the air cuts cold.

sentences.zh: 懷愁戚之多感兮，患涕淚之自零。

translations.literal: Breast laden with sorrow’s many blows—I fear tears falling of themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Sorrow crowds my breast; tears fall unbidden.

sentences.zh: 昔伯瑜之婉孌兮，每綵衣以娛親。

translations.literal: Ancient Boyu was tender—he often donned colored robes to cheer his parents.
translations.idiomatic: Like Boyu of Zhou I ache—he wore bright robes to delight his kin.

sentences.zh: 悼今日之乖隔兮，奄與家為參辰。

translations.literal: I mourn today’s cruel separation—suddenly with family I am Orion and Sirius.
translations.idiomatic: Today’s cruel divide casts kin as stars that never meet.

sentences.zh: 豈相去之云遠兮，曾不盈乎數尋。

translations.literal: How can they say the distance is far—it does not fill a few yards’ span.
translations.idiomatic: We stand mere feet apart yet cannot bridge the gap.

sentences.zh: 何宮禁之清切兮，欲瞻睹而莫因。

translations.literal: How sternly clear are palace barriers—I long to gaze yet find no way.
translations.idiomatic: Palace gates cut sharply—no path opens for my gaze.

sentences.zh: 仰行雲以歔欷兮，涕流射而沾巾。

translations.literal: I lift my eyes to drifting clouds and sigh; tears jet forth soaking my kerchief.
translations.idiomatic: I gaze at clouds and weep; tears stream until my sleeves drip.

sentences.zh: 惟屈原之哀感兮，嗟悲傷于離別。

translations.literal: Only Qu Yuan’s sorrow moves—alas for parting’s grief.
translations.idiomatic: Qu Yuan knew this ache—parting tears fall anew.

sentences.zh: 彼城闕之作詩兮，亦以日而喻月。

translations.literal: Those who made poems at the gate tower likewise paired sun with moon.
translations.idiomatic: The poets at the gate tower likened sun and moon—

sentences.zh: 況骨肉之相於兮，永緬邈而兩絕。

translations.literal: How much more flesh and bone sharing breath—forever distant, severed both ways.
translations.idiomatic: —yet kinship binds tighter than sun and moon, now lost forever.

sentences.zh: 長含哀而抱戚兮，仰蒼天而泣血。

translations.literal: Long bearing sorrow with clasped grief—I lift blue Heaven and weep blood.
translations.idiomatic: Endless sorrow grips me; I lift my eyes to Heaven and weep blood.

sentences.zh: 亂曰：骨肉至親，化為他人，永長辭兮。

translations.literal: Envoi: flesh and bone most dear become strangers—forever gone.
translations.idiomatic: Envoi: closest kin turned stranger—gone forever.

sentences.zh: 慘愴愁悲，夢想魂歸，見所思兮。

translations.literal: Anguish and drear longing—dreaming souls return to show those missed.
translations.idiomatic: Bitter grief—dreaming souls return with remembered faces.

sentences.zh: 驚寤號咷，心不自聊，泣漣洏兮。

translations.literal: Startled awake I wail—the heart finds no ease; tears trickle down.
translations.idiomatic: Waking with a cry the heart finds no rest; tears thread endlessly.

sentences.zh: 援筆舒情，涕淚增零，訴斯詩兮。

translations.literal: I take brush to vent feeling—tears multiply as I speak this poem.
translations.idiomatic: Brush in hand I bare grief; tears fall faster as I write these lines.

sentences.zh: 後為貴嬪，姿陋無寵，以才德見禮。

translations.literal: Later she became honorable lady—plain in looks without favor, honored for talent and virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Raised to honorable lady despite plain looks, she won respect through wit and character.

sentences.zh: 體羸多患，常居薄室，帝每遊華林，輒回輦過之。

translations.literal: Her frame frail and often ill, she dwelt in modest chambers; whenever the emperor toured Splendid Grove he turned his carriage to pass her gate.
translations.idiomatic: Frail and sickly, she kept to spare rooms; each imperial outing to Splendid Grove detoured past her lodge.

sentences.zh: 言及文義，辭對清華，左右侍聽，莫不稱美。

translations.literal: When discourse touched literary meaning her replies were lucid and splendid; attendants left and right listened—none failed to praise.
translations.idiomatic: Her answers on texts sparkled; every listener praised her grace.

sentences.zh: 及元楊皇后崩，芬獻誄曰：

translations.literal: When primal Empress Yang Yuan died, Fen presented a dirge, saying:
translations.idiomatic: When Empress Yang Yan died, Zuo Fen offered a lament:

sentences.zh: 惟泰始十年秋七月丙寅，晉元皇后楊氏崩，嗚呼哀哉！

translations.literal: On the bingyin day of autumn in the seventh month of the tenth Taishi year the Jin primal empress Lady Yang died—alas!
